event: Greenhouse Gas Pollution Pricing Act comes into force, with a consumer fuel charge and an Output-Based Pricing System for large industry
why_it_matters: The industrial half creates the Canadian carbon cost that is deducted from the EU border charge under Article 9

event: Saskatchewan, Ontario and Alberta challenge the Act. Saskatchewan and Ontario appeal courts uphold it; Alberta finds it unconstitutional
why_it_matters: Provincial resistance to carbon pricing is long-standing, not new

event: Federal plan sets the carbon price rising to CAD 170/t by 2030
why_it_matters: The abandoned high-ambition path. Usable as the upper bound of an accelerated scenario

event: Supreme Court of Canada upholds the Act 6-3, ruling minimum national carbon pricing a matter of national concern
why_it_matters: Legal certainty established, which makes the subsequent rollback more striking

event: Consumer fuel charge set to zero. British Columbia and the Northwest Territories drop their own consumer carbon taxes the same day
why_it_matters: The consumer half effectively ends. No direct effect on hydrogen production but it signals political direction

event: Saskatchewan pauses its industrial carbon pricing system
why_it_matters: Erosion reaches the industrial half, which is the half this study depends on

event: Bill C-4 permanently repeals the consumer fuel charge, backdated to April 2025. The industrial system is deliberately retained
why_it_matters: Canada now has an industrial-only carbon price

event: Federal government publishes a revised industrial carbon price path
why_it_matters: Replaces the 170-by-2030 plan and is a direct input to the Article 9 deduction

event: Prices actually paid vary widely by province: credits trade near CAD 65 in British Columbia, 72 in Ontario, and as low as about 37.50 where cheap Alberta credits are available
quantified_effect: Effective price CAD 37.50-72 against the CAD 95 federal benchmark used in the model
why_it_matters: The headline national price is not what a Canadian producer faces. The model uses the benchmark, so it overstates the deduction and understates EU CBAM cost

event: United Kingdom launches its own Emissions Trading Scheme, with a cap 5% below its former share of the EU cap
quantified_effect: Cap set 5% below the former EU share
why_it_matters: The two carbon markets separate. This separation is the foundation of the whole study

event: First United Kingdom carbon auctions take place
The post-Brexit Trade and Cooperation Agreement commits both sides to give serious consideration to linking the two carbon markets
why_it_matters: Reconnection was always possible, just dormant for several years

event: United Kingdom tightens its cap but releases 53 million extra permits between 2024 and 2027 and raises the free allocation share for industry from 37% to 40%
quantified_effect: 53 million extra permits 2024-2027; free allocation share 37% to 40%
why_it_matters: These decisions flooded the market and drove the UK carbon price down

event: United Kingdom and European carbon prices, previously correlated, separate sharply
United Kingdom carbon price reaches a low of GBP 31.48 per tonne
why_it_matters: Below the model's GBP 40 low scenario, so the sensitivity range does not bracket the observed historic floor

event: European carbon permits trade more than 60% above their United Kingdom equivalents
why_it_matters: A cheap UK carbon price became a liability once the EU border mechanism entered its definitive phase, because UK exporters would face the differential at the EU border

event: Press reports that linking talks have begun. The United Kingdom carbon price rises 13% in a single day
why_it_matters: Strong evidence the market treats reconnection as a genuine prospect rather than diplomatic language

event: United Kingdom and European Union announce a Common Understanding covering linking the two carbon markets and potentially exempting each other from their respective border charges
why_it_matters: Basis for the linked UK price variant. Mutual CBAM exemption does NOT touch either modelled corridor, since neither Canada nor China is party

event: United Kingdom confirms shipping will enter its carbon market from July 2026
European Union member states unanimously agree to let the Commission open formal negotiations on linking
why_it_matters: Reconnection moves from idea to formal process

event: United Kingdom opens a consultation on extending its carbon market to half the emissions from international voyages, starting 2028
why_it_matters: This is the fork the model tests in its 2030 projection

event: Free permits for aircraft operators fully withdrawn
The international shipping consultation closes without a final legislative decision
why_it_matters: Why the expansion must be labelled NOT LAW wherever it appears

event: United Kingdom carbon market begins covering shipping, but only voyages between two UK ports and emissions while a vessel sits in a UK port
quantified_effect: 0% of the international voyage; 100% of at-berth and UK-UK
why_it_matters: This is the current baseline in the model. The long voyage from China is not covered

event: United Kingdom carbon border charge takes effect for aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, and iron and steel. It counts only direct process emissions, with indirect emissions from electricity delayed until at least 2029
quantified_effect: Direct emissions only from 2027; indirect emissions from 2029 at the earliest
why_it_matters: Ends the period in which goods landing at Felixstowe face no carbon border cost. NOT YET IMPLEMENTED: the model applies the full embedded emissions figure on the UK corridor in 2027 and 2028, which overstates UK CBAM liability. Needs a direct/indirect split in the emissions table

event: The carbon border charge is negotiated as part of the wider climate package. The final timetable for withdrawing free permits is slower than the Commission originally wanted, after sustained industry lobbying
why_it_matters: The schedule this study treats as fixed was itself a political compromise, and has been softened once already

event: The carbon border regulation formally enters into force
FuelEU Maritime adopted, requiring ships entering European ports to meet greenhouse gas intensity targets with penalties for exceeding them
why_it_matters: One of the six cost components, and it applies only to the Hamburg route

event: Transitional period in which importers report embedded emissions but pay nothing
Shipping begins to be phased into the European carbon market
A simplification package amends the carbon border regulation, easing administrative requirements before the payment phase
why_it_matters: The first amendment, showing the rules can and do change

event: Detailed rules published on how the price of carbon border certificates is calculated
why_it_matters: Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2548

event: Detailed rules published setting the default emissions values applied where an importer does not report verified actual emissions
why_it_matters: Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2621. These defaults are the primary emissions input to the model

event: Commission proposes extending the carbon border charge from 2028 to roughly 180 further products containing large amounts of steel and aluminium, plus anti-avoidance measures
why_it_matters: Direction of travel reverses from simplification back to expansion. Does not touch hydrogen or ammonia, which are already in scope

event: The carbon border charge enters its definitive phase. Importers must buy and surrender certificates
why_it_matters: The baseline year of the study

event: Shipping fully covered by the European carbon market. Voyages between two European ports charged in full; voyages to or from a non-European port charged at half
why_it_matters: The Halifax to Hamburg voyage falls into the 50% category

event: Member states agree their negotiating position on the downstream expansion and require the Commission to review annually whether further products should be added
why_it_matters: The proposal still has to pass the full legislative process

event: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1412 sets revised EU ETS free allocation benchmarks for 2026-2030
why_it_matters: Added by Samir 6 Aug 2026, not in Alex's original timeline. Only bites if the benchmark CBAM mechanism is selected

event: The share of embedded emissions generating a charge reaches 48.5%
why_it_matters: The projection year of the study, sitting just after the steepest single increase

event: Free permits reach zero and the full 100% of embedded emissions generates a charge
why_it_matters: The year the two CBAM mechanisms converge

event: Hydrogen first appears in China's national high technology research plan
why_it_matters: The longest policy history of the four jurisdictions, which makes the slow real-world progress more striking

event: The national five-year plan names hydrogen a strategic industry, focused on fuel cell vehicles
why_it_matters: Attention is on using hydrogen, not on producing it cleanly

event: The national planning commission repeats the fuel cell priority. Five city clusters are selected for demonstration projects with rewards up to CNY 1.7 billion
The National Hydrogen Development Plan is published
China produces and consumes more than 36.5 million tonnes of hydrogen, overwhelmingly from coal
why_it_matters: Enormous scale, overwhelmingly coal-based, which is what keeps the Chinese embedded emissions figure high

event: The national energy authority asks regional governments to steadily develop renewable hydrogen but stops short of a large subsidy programme beyond pilots
why_it_matters: Ambition stated without the funding to accelerate it

event: The State Council and the environment ministry approve a set of five-year environmental plans

The five-year plan for the energy system covering 2026-2030 targets non-fossil fuels at 25% of energy use by 2030 and wind and solar above half of installed capacity, while also calling for coal to be strengthened as guaranteed baseline supply
quantified_effect: Non-fossil 25% of energy use by 2030; wind and solar above 50% of installed capacity
why_it_matters: Both the accelerating and the slowing signal appear in one document, which is the honest basis for treating China's direction as uncertain

event: China launches an efficiency and emissions reduction campaign across nine heavy industries including synthetic ammonia. Capacity failing to meet efficiency standards is to be closed after 2028
why_it_matters: Directly relevant, since ammonia is one of the two modelled products. Would lower the Chinese ammonia emissions intensity from 2029, which the model does not currently represent

event: Hydrogen from coal costs roughly half as much as hydrogen from renewable electricity. Green hydrogen is about 1.4% of national supply. Industry projections suggest cost parity with coal plus carbon capture around 2030
quantified_effect: Green hydrogen about 1.4% of national supply; parity with coal plus CCS around 2030
why_it_matters: The economics, not the policy, are what keep Chinese hydrogen emissions high. This is what the stable scenario assumes continues
